clue.text: Quality work done by southern chap in boats

indicators.note: 'in' places the southern chap inside the boats, splitting that word around him

blocks.note: boats as two words for vessels, CRAFT and SHIP, side by side
S is the standard abbreviation for southern
a chap is a man

explanation.surface: A southern fellow is praised for the fine work he does while out in boats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boats' must supply two separate vessel words, which is easy to miss when looking for one plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Craftsmanship is the skill shown in a well made object, so it names high quality handiwork.

clue.text: Asked again for Queen to return before requested

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the abbreviation for Queen is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword abbreviation for Queen
to have ordered something is to have requested it

explanation.surface: Someone places a second request, asking for the Queen to come back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'before' simply puts the reversed Queen ahead of the second word.
explanation.definitionFit: To reorder goods is to place a fresh request for them, so the past tense means sought once more.

clue.text: Pass off as valuable when love's within grasp

indicators.note: within puts the zero for love inside the word for grasp

blocks.note: a fist is a clenched hand that grasps
love is zero in tennis, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone tries to sell a worthless thing as precious while love is within reach.
explanation.definitionFit: To foist something is to palm it off on someone deceptively, passing a poor article off as worthwhile.

clue.text: Flashing lead holds roof tile

indicators.note: holds says the words before it contain the answer within their run of letters

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Builder's talk: the lead flashing on a roof keeps a tile in place.
explanation.walkthrough: Flashing and lead are genuine roofing materials, which makes the phrase look like a definition rather than the source of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Shingles are thin overlapping slabs of wood or slate used to cover roofs.

clue.text: Harsh to have a Serb, they say, in charge

indicators.note: they say signals that the words before it are to be spoken and heard, not spelt

blocks.note: acerb, an old word for sour, is pronounced like 'a Serb'
IC is the standard abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: Someone complains that it is harsh to have a Serbian placed in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Acerbic remarks are sharp and biting in tone, so the word means harsh or cutting.

clue.text: Amanuensis reveals headless Mary mystery first

indicators.note: headless means the name loses its opening letter
first tells us the mystery word comes ahead of the shortened name

blocks.note: a secret is a mystery
the name taken as written, before its head is removed

explanation.surface: A scribe exposes the mystery of a beheaded Queen Mary.
explanation.walkthrough: The headless Mary evokes Mary Queen of Scots; here it just loses its M.
explanation.definitionFit: An amanuensis is a person employed to take dictation or copy manuscripts, an old word for a clerical assistant.

clue.text: I am bipedal, having poetic feet

indicators.note: having says the opening words contain the answer within them

blocks.note: the letters run from the start of the phrase into the third word

explanation.surface: A creature boasts of walking on two legs and therefore of having feet worthy of a poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a plural of iambus; the clue's feet are metrical units, not body parts.
explanation.definitionFit: An iamb is a metrical unit of one short and one long syllable, and the Latin plural names several of them.

clue.text: Euclid, for example, met a match in A1 form

indicators.note: form as a verb means shape, so the letters are moulded into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
the digit 1 stands for the letter I alongside the A

explanation.surface: The great Greek geometer finally met his equal, someone in top form.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 means first-rate in British slang, but here A and the 1-shaped I are just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Euclid, author of the Elements, is the classic Greek geometry scholar, a specimen of someone who works in numbers.

clue.text: French kiss not to be taken seriously?

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: a deep kiss puts the speaking organ inside a mouth
second meaning: the idiom for ironic or jokey speech

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is playful and literal, hence the question mark; the second is the everyday idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: A remark made with ironic insincerity is described by this idiom, and literally the phrase pictures a French kiss.

clue.text: A bore takes one drink and goes native

indicators.note: takes means the first words absorb the next ones, holding them inside

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
one is the Roman numeral I
gin is a drink

explanation.surface: A tedious person has a gin and goes off to live like the locals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes native' is a stock phrase, but only 'native' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An aborigine is an original inhabitant of a land, someone indigenous to the place.

clue.text: He came over to take part in a small dramatic sketch

indicators.note: to take part in means only a portion of the phrase supplies the letters

blocks.note: the letters are lifted from the middle of the phrase

explanation.surface: An actor comes along to appear in a brief stage skit.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'take part in' sound like acting, which is fitting for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A cameo is a short vivid piece of writing or acting, a brief theatrical vignette.

clue.text: Little girl in hat was done for

indicators.note: in places the girl inside the headgear word

blocks.note: taken as written
Di is a short form of the name Diana

explanation.surface: A small girl wearing a hat was finished off.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal idiom 'had it' describes someone ruined or beyond saving, the same as being finished.

clue.text: Talking rubbish compels use of bigger bin

indicators.note: making use of letters implies putting them to work in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone babbling nonsense insists on getting a larger dustbin.
explanation.definitionFit: Gibbering is rapid unintelligible speech, so it means uttering nonsense.

clue.text: Mum takes right entrance to seaside resort

indicators.note: takes means the mother word picks up the following words after her

blocks.note: ma is an informal word for mum
R is the abbreviation for right
a gate is an entrance

explanation.surface: Mother takes the correct way in to reach the coast.
explanation.walkthrough: MARGATE is a traditional seaside town on the Kent coast of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Margate is a long established English holiday town on the coast, a classic example of a resort.

clue.text: Express regret for driving VW with soldier into choppy sea

indicators.note: driving into means moving inside, so the car and soldier end up within the sea letters
choppy water is churned up, so the sea word is mixed up

blocks.note: the Polo is a car model made by Volkswagen
GI is an American soldier
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone says sorry for driving a Volkswagen, with a soldier on board, into rough water.
explanation.definitionFit: To apologise is to say sorry, putting remorse into words.

clue.text: Church girl in wonderland finds communion vessel

blocks.note: CH is the abbreviation for church
the girl in Wonderland is Lewis Carroll's Alice

explanation.surface: A churchgoing girl in a fantasy land discovers the cup used at Mass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in wonderland' pins down which girl is meant rather than giving letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A chalice is the goblet holding wine at the Eucharist, the cup used in the sacrament.

clue.text: O, it ain't 'im juggling; it ain't real

indicators.note: juggling throws things about, so the letters before it are tossed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophes dropped

explanation.surface: A spectator cries that the performer juggling is not him at all, it is a fake.
explanation.definitionFit: An imitation is a copy or counterfeit, something that is not genuine.

clue.text: Little rod catches baby frog

blocks.note: a tad is a little bit
a pole is a rod

explanation.surface: A small fishing rod lands a young frog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'catches' sounds like a container signal, but the two pieces simply sit side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A tadpole is the larval stage of a frog, so it is the young amphibian.

clue.text: Soft gold carried by the Spanish and French is used for shoulder ornament

indicators.note: something carried by another is held within it, so these letters go inside the Spanish word

blocks.note: el is Spanish for the
p, piano, is the musical direction for soft
Au is the chemical symbol for gold
et is French for and

explanation.surface: A soft gold piece worn by Spanish and French officers serves as decoration on the shoulder.
explanation.definitionFit: An epaulet is the decorative strap or fringed pad on the shoulder of a military uniform.

clue.text: Staying upset is gloomy

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Remaining unhappy is a dismal state.
explanation.definitionFit: Stygian describes the darkness of the river Styx in the underworld, hence very dark and dismal.

clue.text: Crafty curs! They know more then they're telling

definitions.text: They know more then they're telling

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: cunning mongrels

blocks.clueFragment: They know more then they're telling
blocks.note: second meaning: secretive people who keep their knowledge to themselves

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names discreet, knowing people, while literally the phrase pictures cunning hounds.

clue.text: As usual, May courts disaster

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase defining an adjective; 'customary' fits 'as is customary'

indicators.note: a disaster wrecks things, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Typically, a woman called May is flirting with calamity.
explanation.definitionFit: Customary describes what is habitual or normally done, in line with the ordinary routine.

clue.text: "Spotted", said the spider without hesitation

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the hesitation sound is taken out
said tells us to go by what is spoken, so we hear the result rather than spell it

blocks.note: taken as written
hesitation is er; say spider with its closing er sound dropped and you hear a single syllable

explanation.surface: A spider declares without pausing that it has been seen.
explanation.walkthrough: Say the creature's name and drop its final 'er' sound: what is left is pronounced exactly like the answer, though spelt differently.
explanation.definitionFit: To have spied something is to have caught sight of it, glimpsed or observed it.

clue.text: Teach teacher

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb, to train or tutor
second meaning: a noun, a trainer or tutor

explanation.walkthrough: One word serves as both verb and noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A sports trainer or private tutor is called this, and the verb means to instruct someone.

clue.text: Mascot takes tea with the Marines

blocks.note: cha is an informal British word for tea
RM stands for the Royal Marines

explanation.surface: A regimental mascot has a cup of tea with the Marines.
explanation.definitionFit: A charm is a lucky object or talisman, as a mascot is something kept to bring good fortune.

clue.text: I bail out, saying I was somewhere else

definitions.note: a phrase describing the claim the noun names

indicators.note: out suggests the letters are let loose and reassembled differently

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A suspect jumps bail, claiming to have been elsewhere at the time.
explanation.definitionFit: An alibi is a defence that the accused was in another place when the crime happened.

clue.text: Get moving! Don't appear moribund!

blocks.note: first meaning: the command to hurry up
second meaning, read literally: seem to be living, not dying

explanation.walkthrough: Moribund means close to death, so the second sense is the literal reading of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is an order to be quick and alert, and literally asks someone to seem living.

clue.text: Commercial vines met trade disruption

indicators.note: a disruption throws things out of order, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A wine business finds its vineyards hit by an interruption to commerce.
explanation.definitionFit: A commercial, as a noun, is a broadcast promotion, the same thing as a paid promotion on screen.
